examples.note: Worked scenario demonstrating the choice and placement of a researched keyword.

parts.quote: A website helps users become Australian citizens.
You have researched with users who are keen to become Australian citizens. You have found they use the keyword ‘citizen’ a lot.
Include ‘citizen’ in the content, title, meta description and web address (URL).

rules.quote: Match keywords to the search terms people use
rules.violation_condition: Content omits the terminology its intended users are likely to search for, using different terminology instead.
when: Assess the terminology against the intended users and the information or task they are searching for.
rules.why: G-4: the heading and body express one check for expected search terminology, not separate findings.

rules.quote: Structure content (including forms and online tools) so people find what they need.
rules.specification: The page supplies no structural criteria for judging findability. Assessment needs the intended user task and a basis for deciding whether the organisation obstructs it.
rules.violation_condition: The organisation of content prevents users from locating the information they need.
when: Applies to online content, including online forms and tools.
rules.why: G-1: this child instruction concerns content organisation, a different finding from keyword selection or placement.

rules.quote: Include keywords once or twice, if they make sense, in the first paragraph of the content.
rules.violation_condition: The first paragraph contains no relevant keyword even though one could be included naturally.
when: Applies to the first paragraph.
Keywords need only be included where they make sense.
The stated target is one or two uses; excessive repetition is assessed under the keyword-overuse rule.
Including keywords in the final paragraph is optional.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3: retain the natural-use condition and optional final-paragraph use without creating another requirement; keep omission distinct from overuse.

examples.note: Worked scenario illustrating related terminology selected for the topic and users’ needs.

parts.quote: You are writing content to help users find Australian embassies in Europe.
User research shows that when people search for an Australian embassy they’re either:
preparing to travel
needing help with an emergency situation.
The types of keywords you might use are:
embassy locations
emergency terms and current dangers
modes of travel
passport and visa terms.

rules.quote: Include terms and concepts that are closely related to the topic you are writing about.
rules.specification: The page does not define the required breadth of related concepts or how much related terminology is sufficient. Do not invent a minimum count.
rules.violation_condition: Content lacks terms or concepts closely related to its topic.
rules.why: The main test separates missing related terminology from mismatched search terms and from the presence of irrelevant keywords; E-4 forbids inventing a coverage threshold.

covers.quote: Include keywords once or twice, if they make sense, in the first paragraph of the content.

rules.specification: The page gives no general threshold for ‘too many’. Its first-paragraph guidance is once or twice, but it does not specify whether that count is per keyword or for all keywords combined.
rules.violation_condition: Content contains excessive keyword use or repetition.
when: Assess repetition in context rather than imposing an invented keyword-density limit.
For the first paragraph, the stated guidance is one or two uses where they make sense.
rules.why: The main test separates excessive repetition from off-topic keywords; G-2 absorbs the first-paragraph frequency guidance, and E-4 prevents an invented general threshold.

rules.quote: Don’t use too many keywords or keywords that are outside the context of the content.
rules.violation_condition: Content includes keywords unrelated to its context.
when: This check concerns contextual relevance, not the number of keyword occurrences.
rules.why: The main test requires a separate finding for irrelevant keywords: relevance and excessive repetition can be violated independently.

covers.quote: Some information could relate to a specific place or a group of people.

examples.note: Embedded example of including a relevant group and place.

parts.quote: student placements in northern NSW

rules.quote: Make sure you include these details (for example, ‘student placements in northern NSW’).
rules.violation_condition: Content about a particular place or group of people omits the relevant place or group details.
when: Applies when the information relates to a specific place or group of people.
rules.why: G-2: place-specific and group-specific information are conditions of one details-omission check.
